claims.text: Equimolar WTaTiVZr has improved plastic strain and toughness relative to pure tungsten under high-temperature plasma-facing conditions.
Altered grain-boundary chemistry and microstructure govern the proposed improvement in plastic strain and toughness.
Ti, V, and Zr additions encourage grain-boundary segregation or formation of finely dispersed second phases.
The proposed grain-boundary segregation or second phases promote grain-boundary sliding and diffusion-assisted plasticity at elevated temperature.
Grain-boundary sliding and diffusion-assisted plasticity delay crack initiation and brittle fracture.
The initial alloy is equimolar WTaTiVZr in an as-cast and homogenized condition.
Matching grain size, geometry, and pre-test heat treatment between WTaTiVZr and pure tungsten isolates the role of grain-boundary chemistry and microstructure.
Testing at 1000–1200°C in a low-oxygen atmosphere simulates high-temperature plasma-facing service conditions.
Ti, V, and Zr modify the grain-boundary chemistry of WTaTiVZr.
The modified grain-boundary chemistry reduces the propensity for brittle intergranular fracture by facilitating grain-boundary sliding and diffusional creep.
Facilitated grain-boundary sliding and diffusional creep permit elevated-temperature stress redistribution, thereby enhancing plastic deformation and toughness.
The proposed grain-boundary mechanism is not active in pure tungsten because pure tungsten has a more uniform and brittle grain-boundary structure.
WTaTiVZr will exhibit greater plastic strain to failure than pure tungsten under the defined high-temperature conditions.
WTaTiVZr will exhibit greater toughness, measured by area under the stress–strain curve, than pure tungsten.
Post-deformation TEM or EBSD will reveal evidence of active grain-boundary sliding and diffuse dislocation activity in WTaTiVZr that is absent in pure tungsten.
The hypothesis applies when grain-boundary sliding and diffusion creep are thermally activated.
Annealing treatments may alter grain-boundary chemistry and limit the hypothesis's applicability.
Irradiation-dominated behavior may limit the hypothesis's applicability.
